responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character21_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Absolutely—I’ll speak as Character21_F, from her perspective.

Fairness, to me, has always meant more than just treating everyone the same. It’s about acknowledging people’s different starting points and making sure opportunities aren’t reserved only for those who already have advantages. Coming from an upper middle class background, I know I’ve had access to things—good schools, safe neighborhoods, support networks—some people never get. So when I think about fairness, I think about what it takes to actually level the playing field, not just assume it’s already level.

A sense of belonging is huge for me. I’ve always felt at home when people cared enough to try to understand each other, not just tolerate each other. Community is built by people who show up—not just physically, but emotionally. Growing up, I saw how much it mattered when neighbors helped each other, whether it was someone dropping off soup when you were sick or just remembering a birthday. Those small things made me feel connected, and I think real belonging comes from those moments of genuine care.

What stands out most is how much I valued spaces where people could bring their whole selves. I think about my college experience, where there were students from all over—different countries, backgrounds, stories. The places I felt safest and happiest were the ones where difference was seen as a strength, rather than a threat. I’ve always wanted my community—wherever it is—to feel like that: open, welcoming, and fair, even when it means having hard conversations or making changes to include people who have been left out.

Those are the things that matter to me—fairness as equity, belonging as feeling seen, and community as people choosing to care about each other.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character21_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Honestly, sitting in the community garden and seeing so many different kinds of people around makes me feel hopeful and curious. I’ve always believed that a neighborhood is at its best when it brings together people with different stories and perspectives. It’s not just about surface-level diversity—it’s the way those differences can challenge you and help you grow.

Sometimes it’s a little intimidating, I’ll admit, especially if I don’t know the right way to approach someone whose background or experience is really different from mine. But mostly, I feel a responsibility to reach out, even if it’s awkward. I’ve seen how much richer everyday life gets when you actually make those connections—like learning a new recipe from a neighbor who immigrated recently, or just hearing how someone else sees the world. It’s honestly one of the things I find most exciting about where we live.

I do notice, though, that not everyone always feels comfortable mixing or talking openly. There are people who seem isolated, or who keep to themselves because they feel like outsiders, or maybe they’re just tired—life can be hard, especially if you’re dealing with stuff like addiction, illness, or people not accepting your identity or family structure. That makes me feel even more that it matters to reach out and try to make sure no one feels invisible. I know I won’t always get it right, but I want to at least try to be the kind of neighbor who listens and is willing to learn.

So, for me, interacting with all sorts of people in the neighborhood isn’t just something I tolerate—it’s something I value. It’s what makes the place feel alive and real, and it’s a chance to become a better, more understanding person myself.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah, I’m glad you’re bringing this up. I feel like real community only happens when people can show up as who they are—even if that doesn’t fit what’s “normal” or comfortable for everyone else. If someone is living with alcoholism or substance abuse, or has a health condition that needs extra understanding, or if their family just looks different from what we’re used to, I don’t think the answer is to avoid them or act awkward. It’s about finding ways to interact that make everyone feel like they matter.

I think the most important thing is to meet people without judging them first. Like, if I hear someone in the garden speaking a language I don’t know, or see a couple that doesn’t fit the “traditional” mold, my job is to be friendly, make eye contact, and include them in the small stuff—like asking how their day was, or if they want to join in a group activity. It doesn’t have to be complicated; sometimes just being the person who says “hi” can make a big difference.

But I definitely think more communication and tolerance are needed, especially in situations where people’s experiences are really far apart. For example, if someone is struggling with addiction, there’s a lot of stigma, and people can make snap judgments or avoid them altogether—which just makes things worse. I think we all need to be willing to learn about what others are going through and not assume we know their whole story. That goes for health issues, too—sometimes people just need you to listen and not freak out.

There are also times when cultural or religious differences can create misunderstandings. Maybe someone isn’t comfortable with certain foods or ways of dressing, or they celebrate holidays we’re not used to. I think it helps to ask questions respectfully instead of making assumptions, and to create space for people to share what matters to them—like inviting neighbors to talk about their traditions, or making sure community events don’t leave anyone out.

I’m absolutely willing to talk about this stuff, even if it’s uncomfortable, because I don’t want to live in a neighborhood where people feel invisible or unwelcome. If we don’t make an effort to communicate and show tolerance, we just end up with people living side by side who never really know or trust each other. I’d rather take the risk of saying the wrong thing and learn, than stay silent and closed off. That’s the only way community really works, in my opinion.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character21_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s a tough question, but it’s one I’ve thought a lot about. When resources and jobs are tight, fairness doesn’t mean just looking out for people who already have an advantage. At the same time, I get why local residents worry about their own security and opportunities—it’s not wrong to care about your ability to make a living.

For me, fairness means trying to see the bigger picture. Migrant workers often come here because they’re chasing opportunities they don’t have at home, and a lot of times they’re doing the jobs that others aren’t willing to do. At the same time, it’s important we don’t ignore the struggles of people who are already here and feel like their prospects are shrinking.

If I had to find a balance, I’d want policies that protect vulnerable local workers—things like job retraining, education, and fair wages—while also not scapegoating migrants. I think it’s possible to have both: provide pathways for people who want to work and contribute, and also invest in local communities so people don’t feel threatened or left behind. Maybe that means setting reasonable limits in certain situations, or prioritizing jobs where there’s a clear shortage, but I don’t think shutting the door entirely is fair or effective.

And on a community level, I believe in supporting each other. If migrants are part of the neighborhood, they’re contributing to the same schools, economy, and public spaces. The more we see each other as “us,” not “us vs. them,” the less zero-sum it feels. But that only works if we’re honest about the pressures people are feeling, and make sure no one is ignored.

So, bottom line: fairness is about sharing responsibility and opportunity, not just protecting what you have. That means caring for your neighbors—no matter where they’re from—and being willing to adjust policies to reflect real needs, not just fears.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character21_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
As Character21_F, I think all of these perspectives deserve to be heard—even when I personally disagree with some of the underlying assumptions. It’s clear immigration is a complicated topic, and people’s experiences shape how they see it.

I absolutely agree that immigrants fill important roles, especially in areas where there just aren’t enough local workers—agriculture, food service, care work, and tech, for example. In my own life, I’ve seen how much our communities depend on people who weren’t born here, and I think it’s unfair not to recognize that. The argument that immigrants add diversity and energy to society also rings true for me. I love living in places where you can experience different cultures, foods, ideas—it makes life richer and more interesting.

On concerns about security and crime: I think these are often overblown or manipulated, but I try not to dismiss people’s worries out of hand. The actual evidence usually shows immigrants are less likely to commit crimes than native-born citizens, but the fear is real for some people. I think the solution here is more about sharing accurate information and having open dialogue rather than making policy from fear. We should definitely take security seriously, but we shouldn’t use it as a blanket reason to shut people out.

Humanitarian arguments are also really important to me. I feel strongly about offering help to refugees and people fleeing violence or poverty. I see it as part of our responsibility, especially as a country with resources and a history of immigration. Turning our backs on people in desperate situations doesn’t sit right with me.

The fear about immigration impacting jobs and wages is more complicated. I do think some industries and communities feel the strain more than others, and it’s important not to ignore that. But again, the evidence is mixed—a lot of studies show immigrants actually help the economy overall, though some local impacts can be negative in the short term. This is an area where we need good data and honest conversations, not just slogans.

So, in summary:  
- The arguments about labor shortages, cultural vitality, and humanitarian responsibility make sense to me, and I support them.  
- Security concerns need to be addressed with facts, not just fear, and with targeted, not blanket, solutions.  
- The economic worries are valid for some people and should be talked about honestly, using evidence to guide policy.  
- Where I think more evidence and dialogue are needed is in understanding the real local impacts—what’s helping, what’s hurting, and how we can respond in ways that are fair and humane.

I guess I just want policies that are based on reality and empathy, not panic or prejudice. And I want us to keep talking—even when it’s uncomfortable—because shutting down conversation just creates more division.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character21_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
If I’m being true to my views as Character21_F, I wouldn’t support either extreme—neither complete openness without any criteria nor a total shutdown to workers from other countries. Both seem too rigid and disconnected from reality.

I lean toward a combination of admitting people based on job demand and setting clear, humane numerical limits, while also making specific provisions for refugees and humanitarian cases. Here’s why:

Basing admission on job demand makes sense because it reflects what the economy actually needs. If there are real shortages—like in healthcare, tech, or agriculture—then letting people in to fill those jobs helps everyone. It’s practical and addresses the concerns of local workers who might otherwise feel threatened. But I’d want those job criteria to be fair, not just about filling the lowest-paid or hardest jobs with people who have the fewest rights. Protections and opportunities need to be built in for both immigrants and local workers.

Setting reasonable numerical limits also seems necessary, if only because completely open borders aren’t something most societies are ready for, and there are real concerns about public resources and integration. But those limits should be flexible—able to adapt to changing realities, like economic needs or humanitarian crises—and set with input from different communities, not just top-down.

I feel strongly that there always needs to be space for refugees and people fleeing danger, regardless of quotas or job demand. That’s a moral responsibility.

Social integration matters to me a lot. To make policies work, we need to actually invest in integration—language classes, support for newcomers, and anti-discrimination efforts. Otherwise, even well-designed policies won’t help build a real sense of belonging.

So, my ideal policy would be:  
- Admit immigrants based on transparent job market needs  
- Set adaptable, fair numerical limits  
- Always reserve capacity for refugees and family reunification  
- Invest in integration programs for both newcomers and the communities receiving them

That feels like the most balanced way to combine fairness, practicality, and humanity—staying true to our values while being thoughtful about the challenges.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character21_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character21_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Thank you for asking. Honestly, stepping into Character21_F’s shoes made me appreciate even more how much nuance and empathy she brought to these topics. I always knew she cared about fairness and inclusion, but trying to really think and respond as she would—drawing from her background and her way of reasoning—helped me see how deeply those values shaped her approach to complicated issues like immigration.

One thing I realized is that, for Character21_F, the personal and the political were always connected. Her understanding of fairness came from her own life experiences and privileges, and she was very aware of how those shaped her views. She didn’t shy away from tough questions or the messy parts of community life—she looked for practical policies, but she also insisted on compassion and dialogue.

Embodying her voice made me reflect on my own views, too. I think I sometimes focus more on the policy details or the “big picture,” but she reminded me that it really matters how policies feel on the ground, to real people. Her openness to difference and her willingness to engage—even when it was uncomfortable—make me want to do better at listening and making space for those conversations in my own life.

So, I definitely gained a deeper sense of how lived experience can inform both empathy and realism in policy. And I feel even more convinced that immigration debates need both: practical solutions and a strong moral compass. It’s made me appreciate Character21_F’s legacy, and it’s a reminder to keep those values alive in my own thinking and actions.
